newsitem.title: UK: U.S. Treasury bonds stalled despite Greenspan lift.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasury bonds stalled despite Greenspan lift.

text.p: Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan may have quelled prospects for a near-term U.S. interest rate rise but U.S. government bonds were unlikely to run far with his comments, analysts said on Wednesday.
His testimony to the U.S. Senate on Tuesday, while voicing concerns about wages, reinforced the view the U.S. economy could continue at a good clip without generating excessive inflation.
Such a scenario would usually be perfect for bonds but analysts said it will do little to shift the long bond out of the nearly one point range it has waded in for almost a year.
More exciting gains were to be found elswhere.

"Our overall assessment is the bond will continue to range trade between 6.5 and 7.0 percent for some little while," said Robin Marshall, chief economist at Chase in London. "When you look back that's where we've been for most of the last year."
At 1200 GMT, the benchmark long bond was quoted at 96-16/32 yielding 6.79 percent, up from around a low of around 6.43 percent in March last year and a high of 7.31 percent last July.
Analysts said the Fed Chairman's speech to the Senate Budget Committee was classic Greenspan, soothing inflation concerns with one sentence and stoking them with another.

He said the economy had retained "considerable vigour", with few signs of the imbalances and inflationary tensions that have disrupted past expansions. But he also said the recent period of subdued wage growth may already be running its course.

"He left the market guessing as to what policy would be but the market was relieved there wasn't more in the speech that could have raised interest rate tensions," said Adam Chester, international bond strategist at Yamaichi International Europe.
"It was important for what he didn't say rather for what he did say," said Chester in London.
On balance, Chester and Marshall said Greenspan's speech reduced the chances of a rate rise at the next Federal Open Market Committee Meeting on February 4 and 5.
Neither of them saw a rise in 1997.
However, the fourth quarter employment cost index (ECI) next Tuesday could prove tricky.

"That's the only real anxiety for them," said Marshall. "To date, we have not seen any real evidence of that hitting final prices. We feel we will need to see those numbers in final inflation before they react."
Chester said bond markets could be in for a repeat of last year's scenario with rate tensions building through the spring only to subside in the summer.
This could eventually produce a smart rally in the market, pushing the yield on the long bond to 6.0 percent by year's end.
But Marshall was not so optimistic, seeing a tighter range.

"The curve is pretty flat. When you look down to the long end you don't have an awful lot of yield pick up from the very short end," he added. "You don't have the carry that you have in the European markets."
He preferred British gilts and Spanish and Portuguese bonds.
Doug Jones, senior investment manager at Gartmore, a unit of NatWest Investment Management, with around $12 billion in fixed income under management, would avoid Treasuries altogether.
Jones read more into Greenspan's wage comments than the market has so far. "I find the (market) reaction rather surprising. He did give hints on inflation risks," said Jones.
He too would be watching the ECI closely.

"If we've got a combination of four percent wages growth, four percent employment cost growth, and perhaps four percent GDP growth, it seems to me the risks are on the side of tightening, and earlier rather than later," Jones said.
